restatements.text: Defines terms for the Billionaire Tax Act, including who qualifies as an applicable individual or trust, and establishes January 1, 2026, as the tax obligation date and December 31, 2026, as the valuation date.

Grants the Franchise Tax Board authority to adopt regulations, suspends the Administrative Procedure Act for such rulemaking until 2028, extends the statute of limitations to 10 years for assessing deficiencies for the 2026 tax year, and directs the Board to create new asset reporting forms.
Allows the Legislature to amend the Act by a two-thirds vote, provided the amendments are consistent with and further the Act's purposes.
States that the Act's provisions are severable, and directs courts to preserve the tax by adjusting dates or periods if necessary to cure a constitutional defect.

Imposes 20% and 40% penalties for substantial or gross tax understatements, creates economic substance and anti-avoidance rules allowing the Board to disregard transactions or entities, permits the Board to hire outside experts, and allows the Board to seek a trial de novo in court if it disagrees with the Office of Tax Appeals.
Requires the Act's provisions to be liberally construed to effectuate its purposes.

Creates an expedited validation action in Sacramento County Superior Court to resolve facial validity challenges, mandates direct appeal to the California Supreme Court, and requires such actions to be filed within 60 days of voter approval.
Denies any deduction for state net worth taxes when calculating state income taxes.
Declares that if another measure appearing on the same ballot affecting net worth taxes receives fewer votes, its conflicting provisions shall be void.

Grants the proponent and any citizen the standing to intervene or sue to defend the Act's legality, and requires the Attorney General's funds to promptly cover defense costs if the Attorney General does not defend the Act.

evidence.quote: (k) General anti-avoidance rule. (l) If the Board determines that a transaction or series of transactions lack economic substance, or that a substantial purpose for any transaction or series of transactions was to obtain a tax benefit with respect to this Part that is not intended by the voters or the Legislature, the Board may determine the tax consequences to any person in a manner that is reasonable in light of all the facts and circumstances in order to deny such benefit.
evidence.why: It introduces complex, highly subjective "economic substance" tests to the tax code, allowing the tax board to retroactively alter the tax consequences of transactions.

evidence.quote: (b) “Applicable trust” means any trust (other than a grantor trust or tax-exempt trust), whether or not such trust is a California resident, if an applicable individual still living with net worth of $1 billion ($1,000,000,000) or more (or any entity that would constitute a related person with respect to such individual) has transferred property to such trust.
evidence.why: It adds complex definitions requiring tracing of past property transfers from wealthy individuals to assess taxes.

evidence.quote: (e) No deduction shall be allowed for any tax imposed by the State on net worth, including the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act (Part 27 of this Code) notwithstanding any other provision of law
evidence.why: By denying an income tax deduction for a wealth tax specifically targeting billionaires, it ensures the highest earners pay a larger overall share of taxes.

evidence.quote: (c) Within six months after passage, the Board shall promulgate the forms required for taxpayers to pay the tax imposed by this Part. Those forms may provide for taxpayer attachments demonstrating compliance. The Board shall amend the Personal Income Tax Forms, and amend or create other forms as necessary, for the reporting of assets or other information useful for the implementation of this Part.
evidence.why: It requires the state tax agency to design forms that collect more detailed information about individuals' personal assets and finances.

evidence.quote: (b) The Board shall have the authority to adopt regulations to implement, interpret, make specific, or otherwise carry out any provision of this Part.
evidence.why: It grants the state tax board new regulatory powers to interpret and implement the wealth tax.

evidence.quote: (j) Notwithstanding any other provisions of law, the Board is authorized to hire and pay reasonable fees to any outside experts or outside counsel as appropriate to help fully administer and collect the tax authorized by this part.
evidence.why: It expands the state tax board's power to hire and fund outside experts and counsel for tax collection.

evidence.quote: (3) Notwithstanding Section 19057 or any other law, every notice of a proposed deficiency assessment under this part in regards to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and before January 1, 2027, shall be mailed to the taxpayer within ten years after the return was filed.
evidence.why: It increases the compliance burden by extending the period during which taxpayers can be audited and assessed deficiencies to a full ten years.

evidence.why: It removes standard legislative checks on agency rulemaking, granting more unchecked power to the appointed tax board.

evidence.why: It delegates broad, discretionary authority to an appointed board to reallocate assets and disregard entities.

evidence.why: It denies individuals the ability to deduct state net worth taxes from their state income tax, thereby increasing total taxes paid by those individuals.

evidence.why: By denying an income tax deduction for a wealth tax that targets only billionaires, it causes overall tax rates to become more unequal across different income levels.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure creates legal definitions, administrative procedures, and strong anti-avoidance rules for a new billionaire net worth tax. It sets 20% to 40% penalties for understatements, extends the statute of limitations to 10 years for 2026, denies state income tax deductions for the net worth tax, creates an expedited validation action, and gives citizens standing to defend the law.

Costs include extensive compliance costs for affected taxpayers to navigate subjective "economic substance" doctrines and lengthy potential 10-year audits. Direct costs include state funding allocated for proponents to defend the measure in court. Opportunity costs may include capital flight or delayed business transactions.

Targeted billionaires bear the financial costs of the tax and its compliance burden. The state benefits from expanded regulatory power. Proponents benefit by gaining direct legal standing to defend the act, with their legal costs guaranteed by the state.

Wealthy individuals will likely attempt to restructure assets or challenge the economic substance doctrines in court. The expedited validation action and direct appeal to the Supreme Court ensure prompt, high-stakes litigation over the measure's constitutionality. The Franchise Tax Board may aggressively utilize its temporary exemption from the Administrative Procedure Act to establish stringent rules.

Problem: Wealth taxes are notoriously difficult to enforce because wealthy individuals can use complex entities to obscure ownership. Mechanism: The measure grants the Franchise Tax Board broad regulatory power, suspends the Administrative Procedure Act for initial rulemaking, codifies an "economic substance" doctrine to disregard transactions, imposes up to 40% penalties, and allows a 10-year audit window.

Problem: Novel tax laws face immediate legal challenges that create years of uncertainty. Mechanism: The measure provides an expedited validation action in Sacramento Superior Court with direct review by the Supreme Court, and explicitly grants proponents standing to defend it using state funds.

The Franchise Tax Board gains significant discretionary power to define abusive transactions, disregard business entities, and sue its own appellate body. Proponents and citizens gain power to intervene and defend the measure using state funds.

It is disputed. Scholars disagree on whether a wealth tax with such aggressive anti-avoidance features, 10-year audit windows, and retrospective assessments can be practically enforced, or if it will primarily lead to capital flight and prolonged, expensive litigation.

High administrative losses are likely. Enforcing the "economic substance" rule, assessing the fair market value of complex non-public assets, and identifying "abusive transactions" will require specialized external experts and lead to lengthy, expensive audits and legal battles.

It is a statutory measure that allows the Legislature to amend it only by a two-thirds vote, and only if the amendment is consistent with and furthers the Act's purposes. Otherwise, it requires another ballot measure.
